title: Room and Cellar
premise: Mirabel Thornbury's late-night call-in show begins receiving voices from listeners who died the week before, and her refusal to believe curdles into terror when her childhood imaginary friend appears on her porch, unchanged after forty years. The friend leads her back to the house on Vesper Lane where, in 1974, eight-year-old Mirabel survived by letting something take her brother's name—and her memory of it. As the last resident prepares to sign the sale papers that will seal the house's hunger into a new family, Mirabel must return what was taken: confess the swap aloud, give back the name, and accept that the girl who walked out in 1974 was never entirely her. In the cellar, she surrenders her borrowed identity; the house releases its dead, and Mirabel—now a stranger even to herself—signs nothing, walks away unseen at last, and lets the real Thomas Thornbury finally rest.
about_author: Theo Yarrow is the pen name of a former small-town radio producer who spent a decade reading obituaries on air before turning to fiction. They write horror about the bargains ordinary people make and never admit to.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. During her overnight radio shift, callers describe their own funerals with intimate accuracy; station records confirm they died days ago. She blames a prank, a hoaxer, grief-crazed fans—but one caller hums a lullaby only her mother sang. The beat is denial sharpening into dread as the studio lights flicker and every caller signs off with the same phrase: 'Come home, Miri.'

chapters.title: The Friend on the Porch
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waits on her porch exactly as she left him in 1974—same overalls, same missing tooth. He doesn't threaten; he simply insists she return to Vesper Lane before 'the papers are signed.' Flashbacks fracture her certainty about her brother Thomas's death. The beat is the collapse of her identity as the rational survivor.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, intercut with 1974. Inside the abandoned house, Wren shows her the cellar door she's repressed for decades: the thing below offered eight-year-old Miri survival if someone else took her place, and she chose her brother's name instead of her own. The new buyers arrive early to sign. The beat is horrified recognition—the climax where Mirabel realizes the house has been calling its debt home.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In the cellar, with the buyers' pens hovering over contracts upstairs, Mirabel speaks the confession aloud and offers back the stolen name. The house takes not her life but her false self; the dead callers go silent mid-sentence, released. Wren fades, finally finished. The beat is bleak peace: Mirabel walks out unnamed and unremembered, invisible at last—and free.
